name: CN Tower
label: CN Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Roundhouse Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Roundhouse Park' (way/197447516): middle (336 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/368385388: the OpenStreetMap point 'CN Tower Edge Walk'.

text.description: The CN Tower is Toronto's signature landmark, a 553.3-metre communications and observation tower that was completed in 1976. It stands on the former Railway Lands in downtown Toronto, and its name comes from Canadian National, the railway company that built it. For 32 years, from 1975 until 2007, it was the world's tallest free-standing structure. It still photographs well because of its simple outline: one slender concrete shaft, a pod near the top and a thin antenna above. Up close it is almost too tall to fit in a phone frame, so the trick is to step back. Roundhouse Park is a short walk from the base, with open space around you and room to include the whole tower from bottom to antenna. Keep the phone upright, use the gridlines to line the shaft up with a vertical line, and leave a little sky above the antenna. A bit of the park, a path or a bench in the lower part of the frame gives a sense of scale. If you want a second angle, Harbourfront Park on the waterfront offers a symmetrical view across open lawns. Please be aware that the observation levels are a paid attraction, and the tower itself is not visible from inside it.
text.geographic_location: The CN Tower is in downtown Toronto, on the former Railway Lands just south of Front Street and close to the Harbourfront. Roundhouse Park sits a short walk south-east of the tower's base.
text.directions_text: From Union station (Line 1 subway), the tower is about 11 minutes on foot to the south-west, and St. Andrew station (Line 1 subway) is about 10 minutes away. By streetcar 509, get off at Rees Street, about 7 minutes on foot from the tower, or at Harbourfront Centre, about 9 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole tower in one frame, then try the default lens (1x) for a cleaner look with less stretching at the edges. Telephoto (2x-5x) is good for a close-up of the pod and antenna.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Roundhouse Park (a short walk south of the tower, away from its base). The whole tower fits in frame from a little distance, with room to use a wide-angle lens. From there the tower is to the north-west, and standing back from its base lets the full structure fit in the frame, with space around you away from the busiest crowds near the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright, switch on the gridlines and keep the tower's shaft on one vertical line so it doesn't lean. Leave a little sky above the antenna and use the park's grass or paths at the bottom of the frame. For a different view, Harbourfront Park gives a direct, symmetrical line of sight to the tower across open lawns.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the shaft keeps its detail. Wipe the lens first, as ultra-wide shots show smudges easily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually means softer light and fewer people. At dusk, steady your phone and use night mode for the tower against the darkening sky.

text.access_note: Roundhouse Park is a free, open-air public park, but check for construction or event closures before you go; the tower's observation levels are a separate attraction, so check the official site before you go.

Ultra-wide lenses can stretch objects near the edge of the frame.

name: Casa Loma
label: Casa Loma
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Austin Terrace' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Austin Terrace nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/198471666: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Casa Loma' (95 m across).

text.description:
Casa Loma is a Gothic Revival, castle-style mansion on a hill in midtown Toronto. It was built between 1911 and 1914 as a home for the financier Sir Henry Pellatt, to designs by the architect E. J. Lennox. With 98 rooms, it was the largest private residence in Canada when it was built, and it now operates as a museum. It sits 66 metres above Lake Ontario, which is why the towers and battlements stand out so clearly above the neighbouring streets.

It photographs well because the stonework, turrets and towers give you plenty of shapes to work with, and the quiet, tree-lined residential street in front gives a pleasing setting. From Austin Terrace you can frame the front of the castle without going inside, with the towers rising above the trees. If you want a different feel, the Baldwin Steps climb the slope towards the castle's western side, and Spadina Park shows the building on its grassy rise with more space around it.

The formal front gardens are not open all year, and the view from the top of the towers needs a ticket, so keep your plans flexible. Take a few frames from the street first, then decide whether to go in. Wipe your phone lens before you start, as city dust and fingerprints show up as haze on pale stonework.
text.geographic_location: Casa Loma stands on a hill in midtown Toronto, north-west of Dupont station and north of Spadina Road. Austin Terrace is the quiet residential street beside it.
text.directions_text: The easiest way is to take the Line 1 subway to Dupont station. The castle is north-west of the station, about 6 minutes on foot. Alternatively, take the Line 2 subway or streetcar 512 to Bathurst station, then walk north-east for about 8-10 minutes. Head up the hill, and the castle's towers will guide you the rest of the way. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole front of the castle. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is narrow and you cannot fit the towers in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for towers, windows and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Austin Terrace (street-side view looking southeast at the castle's front). The castle's front facade framed by the tree-lined residential street, with the building's towers and stonework in view. Keep to the pavement and stay clear of driveways.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a tower up with a vertical grid line so the walls don't lean. Let the trees and the street frame the castle at the sides. For a different angle, try the Baldwin Steps, which lead up towards the castle's western side, or Spadina Park for the castle on its grassy slope. Check both positions on the map first.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out and the walls keep their colour. Take a few shots at 0.5x, 1x and 2x so you can pick the best one later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Try mid to late afternoon, when the front of the castle may catch softer light. Trees along the street can screen the building when in leaf, so you may get a clearer view of the stonework in late autumn, winter or early spring.

text.access_note: The castle's exterior can be photographed from the public street, but the front gardens are open only part of the year (May to October), the tower views need paid admission, and professional or wedding shoots need a permit, so check the official site before you go.

Trees along Austin Terrace may partly screen the castle when in leaf.

name: Royal Ontario Museum (the Crystal)
label: Royal Ontario Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bloor Street West and Queen's Park' (4 web pages); placed at crossing of Bloor Street West and Queen's Park (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4942687: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Royal Ontario Museum' (217 m across).
notes: Photographed from outside: the Michael Lee-Chin Crystal.

text.description:
The Royal Ontario Museum is one of the largest museums in North America, and its Michael Lee-Chin Crystal is the part that stops people on the pavement. Daniel Libeskind designed it as a cluster of tilted, angular prisms of aluminium and glass. It was added to the older stone museum building, which opened in 1914, and the Crystal's architectural opening took place on 2 June 2007. The pairing is why it photographs so well: sharp modern shapes sit right up against heavy, rounded stonework, and both fit in one frame.

From there you look south across the Crystal's northern face, with the older stone wing beside it. The contrast between old and new reads most clearly from this spot. Dusk is the favourite time, when the lit glass glows against the darkening sky.

The museum is also being renovated at the moment, with work continuing into 2026, so parts of the building may look different from older pictures. There you can see the Crystal's angles and the north front of the East Wing together along the line of the street. Watch for pedestrians and keep your phone close to you on a busy pavement.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Toronto's University district, just north of Queen's Park and next to the University of Toronto's St. George campus. Its main entrance is on Bloor Street West.
text.directions_text: Take the Line 1 subway to Museum station, whose north-western entrance serves the museum directly. Alternatively, get off at St. George (Line 1 subway or Line 2 subway) and walk east, roughly 4-5 minutes (about 340 m). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the Crystal beside the older stone wing. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole tilting form in one frame from the pavement. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close shots of the angled glass and edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Bloor Street West and Queen's Park (sidewalk at the southwest corner, looking across the Crystal's northern face). The angled aluminum-and-glass prisms of the Crystal rising over Bloor Street, set against the older stone wing of the museum. As an alternative, try Bloor Street West and Avenue Road for the Crystal's sharp angles and the East Wing's north front along the street line.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line up the stone wing and the Crystal so each fills about half the frame, to show the contrast between old and new. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines don't lean too much, and use 0.5x only when you can't fit the whole building in at 1x. From the Avenue Road corner, use the line of the street as a lead-in towards the Crystal.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the lit part of the glass to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright panels don't wash out. At dusk, turn on night mode and hold the phone steady against a lamp post or your own arms to keep the lines sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk, when the lit glass glows against the darkening sky.

text.access_note: The Crystal can be photographed from the public sidewalks outside; check the museum's official site for entry and photography rules before going inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Bloor Street West is a busy pavement with pedestrians and traffic.
Renovation work may mean some parts of the building look different from older pictures.
Holding the phone steady against a lamp post helps keep night shots sharp.
Ultra-wide (0.5x) lenses can make vertical lines lean, so keeping the phone level helps.

name: St. Lawrence Market
label: St. Lawrence Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Front Street East' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Front Street East nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24626769: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
St. Lawrence Market is a busy food market in the St. Lawrence neighbourhood of downtown Toronto. For photographs, the most useful view is the main South Market building on the south side of Front Street East. Its brick façade and arched windows make a solid, balanced frame, and the street in front adds some life to the picture. On a market day, people walking past give the shot a sense of scale and activity.

One thing to know before you go: the North Market building was rebuilt and reopened in 2025, so it may look different from older photos you have seen online. Saturday mornings are the busiest and most colourful time, but the crowds can block a clean view of the building. If you want a quieter frame of the architecture, aim for an early weekday morning.

For a second picture, walk to Wellington Street East. From there the market and the neighbourhood sit in the foreground, with the downtown skyline rising behind. The flatiron Gooderham Building is close by and can fit into the same frame. Keep the phone level so the façade doesn't lean, and take a few frames as people move through the scene. The interior is dim, so treat this as an outdoor photo stop and check current access and any construction on Front Street before you set off.
text.geographic_location: In the St. Lawrence neighbourhood of downtown Toronto, on Front Street East, with the Gooderham Building a short walk away.
text.directions_text: The nearest Line 1 subway stop is King station, about 500 m away, roughly a 6-minute walk, with the market to the east. You can also take streetcar 503 to Wellington Street East, about 3 minutes on foot to the east. From Union station (about 780 m) it is roughly a 10-minute walk, with the market to the north-east of the station. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the façade and the street in front of it. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if crowds or the pavement force you too close, and keep the phone level. Try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the arched windows and brickwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Front Street East (south side, across from the South Market's main façade). The market's brick façade and arched windows with the street and weekend crowds in front, framed for a street-level shot. Look towards the south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building's edges up with them so the façade stays straight. Leave a little street in the bottom of the frame to show the market atmosphere. For a different view, walk to Wellington Street East and shoot with the neighbourhood in front and the downtown skyline behind, including the Gooderham Building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the brick keeps its colour. Take a few shots in a row when people are walking past, then pick the clearest one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning on a weekday gives the cleanest frames. Saturday mornings are the most colourful, but crowds can block the view.

text.access_note: The street viewpoint is on a public street, but check current access and any construction on Front Street East before you go, and check the official site for market visiting details.
claims_not_in_sources: Keeping the phone level and using gridlines helps stop the building's vertical lines from leaning.
Lowering the exposure slider can help keep brick colour when the sky behind is bright.
Taking several frames in a row helps catch a moment when fewer people are in the shot.

name: Hockey Hall of Fame building
label: Hockey Hall of Fame
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Our Game' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Yonge Street and Front Street West (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/62255416: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hockey Hall of Fame' (43 m across).
notes: The 1885 bank building outside; the exhibits inside are not the subject.

text.description:
The Hockey Hall of Fame is Toronto's museum of ice hockey, and its stone-fronted home sits on the corner of Yonge and Front Streets. It forms part of Brookfield Place and includes the historic Bank of Montreal building, which gives the corner its grand, old-fashioned look. This location opened on 18 June 1993. Inside, the exhibition space covers 4,700 square metres, though for this spot you only need the street outside.

The building photographs well because of the bronze 'Our Game' sculpture on the corner. It shows players leaping over the boards, and guides call it one of the most photographed sights in Toronto. Standing by it gives you a ready-made foreground. The carved stone facade fills the background, so the shot has a clear subject up close and plenty of architecture behind it.

If you want a second angle, walk to Yonge Street. From there the corner building angles towards you, and the Bank of Montreal facade and its rooftop dome show up the street. Front Street West gives a diagonal view of the carved stonework and the street-level entrance. Take your time at each, as pavements here can be busy. Exterior renovations were reported in mid-2024, so scaffolding or hoarding may cover part of the facade. Check current conditions before you go, and be ready to shift your angle if something is in the way.
text.geographic_location: The building is in downtown Toronto, at the north-west corner of Yonge Street and Front Street, within Brookfield Place. It is a short walk from Union station and King station.
text.directions_text: From King station (Line 1 subway), the building is to the south, about 3 minutes on foot. From Union station (Line 1 subway) it is to the north-east, about 4 minutes on foot. Streetcar 509 stops at Union Station, about 3 minutes on foot away, and streetcar 503 stops at Yonge Street, King Station, about 4 minutes on foot away. Once you reach the corner of Yonge and Front, look for the bronze sculpture outside the building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the sculpture with the facade behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if pavement space is tight, and keep the phone level so the stonework doesn't lean. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for carved details across the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Yonge Street and Front Street West (outside the building on the corner, by the bronze sculpture). The bronze 'Our Game' sculpture of players leaping over the boards in the foreground, with the Hall's stone facade behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the sculpture low in the frame and let the facade fill the space behind it. Turn on gridlines and place the players on one of the lower lines. For a different view, try Yonge Street, where the corner building angles towards you with the Bank of Montreal dome up the street. Front Street West gives a diagonal view of the carved stonework and entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sculpture to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bronze and the pale stone both keep their detail. Take a few frames, as people often walk through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is likely to be quieter on the pavement. The Yonge Street side faces east, so morning light should fall on it. Whatever the time, check the facade is not covered by scaffolding.

text.access_note: The sculpture and facade can be photographed from the public pavement, but the museum inside is a paid-entry space, so check the official site before you go.

name: Distillery District
label: Distillery District
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'LOVE sculpture at Trinity Street and Tank House Lane' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Trinity Street and Tank House Lane (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/379296804: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Distillery District' (460 m across).

text.description: The Distillery District is a car-free quarter of brick-paved lanes and Victorian factory buildings on the lower east side of downtown Toronto. It was once the Gooderham and Worts Distillery, founded in 1832. Today more than forty heritage buildings across about 13 acres hold cafés, galleries, shops and restaurants. It is described as the largest collection of Victorian-era industrial architecture in North America, and it became a National Historic Site of Canada in 1988. The photos work because everything is built from the same warm brick, and there are no cars to spoil the frame. The big red LOVE sculpture on the corner of Trinity Street and Tank House Lane is the district's best-known photo. Its bright colour stands out against the dark warehouse walls, with the cobbled lanes leading away behind it. Trinity Street is the widest street and often works as a small public square, so there is room to step back and fit the whole scene in. Weekday mornings are calmest. Weekends and the Winter Village season (roughly November to early January) bring much bigger crowds, especially later in the day. If you have time, walk on to the corner of Mill Street and Trinity Street for a view of several old distillery buildings together, or to Case Goods Lane for a narrow brick lane with string lights overhead.
text.geographic_location: The Distillery District sits on the lower east side of downtown Toronto. It is bordered by Parliament Street to the west, Mill Street to the north and Cherry Street to the east.
text.directions_text: The nearest Line 1 subway station is King, about 24 minutes on foot, with the district to the east. By streetcar, get off at Lower River Street (streetcar 503), about 13 minutes on foot, and walk south. Sackville Street (streetcars 306, 501, 503, 505 and 506) is about 15 minutes on foot, also with the district to the south. Once inside, head for the corner of Trinity Street and Tank House Lane. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the sculpture, the brick walls and the lane in one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Try 2x for tighter shots of brick details and the sculpture's shape.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Trinity Street and Tank House Lane (by the large red LOVE sculpture on the corner). The big red LOVE sculpture in front of the brick warehouse walls, framed by the cobblestone lanes. From here your photo shows the red sculpture against the brick warehouse walls, framed by the cobbled lanes. The middle of the district lies a short way to the south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the sculpture on one third of the frame, with the brick walls and lane filling the rest. Crouch slightly to keep the sculpture clear of passers-by. If you want something different, walk to the corner of Mill Street and Trinity Street, where several old distillery buildings come together in one view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sculpture to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the red stays rich and the brick does not wash out. Keep the phone level so the building edges stay straight. In the evening, use night mode on Case Goods Lane and hold the phone steady against a wall or rail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Weekday mornings, before the lanes fill with shoppers and brunch crowds. Evenings suit the lit-up lanes, but they are busier.

text.access_note: The lanes are restricted to pedestrians and cyclists and are generally open to walk through, but check the official site before you go for events, market days and any rules on professional shoots.

name: Kensington Market
label: Kensington Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Garden Car' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Augusta Avenue and Oxford Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/11879671: large area 'Kensington Market' (1034 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
Kensington Market is a lively, mixed neighbourhood just west of Chinatown, packed with small shops, cafés and painted storefronts. It was named a National Historic Site of Canada in November 2006. The writer Robert Fulford said in 1999 that the market had probably been photographed more often than any other place in Toronto. In the 1920s it was known as the Jewish Market, and later waves of newcomers from Portugal, the Caribbean, East Asia and Latin America added to its mix of food and shopfronts. Today you also see many Victorian row houses between the shops.

For photos, start at the Garden Car, the mural-covered old car with plants growing out of it. Guides treat it as the market's unofficial mascot. Behind it you get the bright painted fronts that make the area so easy to shoot on a phone. The car is only there in warmer months, so it may be missing in winter. Check before you go. The best street scenes run along Augusta Avenue and nearby Nassau Street, Baldwin Street and Kensington Avenue. If the car is away, the same colourful frontages still make good pictures. For a different view, Graffiti Alley is full of murals, and the Kensington Parking Garage looks over the low rooftops towards the CN Tower. Murals change often, so a wall you saw online may look different.
text.geographic_location: Kensington Market is in Downtown Toronto, west of Spadina Avenue and Chinatown, between College Street to the north and Dundas Street West to the south. Its main shopping streets are Augusta Avenue, Nassau Street, Baldwin Street and Kensington Avenue.
text.directions_text: The nearest streetcar stop is Augusta Avenue (streetcar 306, streetcar 501 and streetcar 506), about 4 minutes on foot from the market, which lies to the north of the stop. From St. Patrick on the Line 1 subway, walk west for about 1 km. From Queen's Park (Line 1 subway, streetcar 306 and streetcar 506), walk south-west for about 1 km. The Garden Car is the recommended subject near there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) at the Garden Car so the car and the painted storefronts behind it sit naturally together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) in narrow Graffiti Alley, where you can't step back. At the Kensington Parking Garage, use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pull the CN Tower closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Augusta Avenue and Oxford Street (at the corner, on the mural-covered car). The mural-covered old car with plants growing out of it, with the market's painted storefronts behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the car on one third of the frame, with the colourful shopfronts filling the rest. Keep your phone level so the buildings don't lean. If you have time, Graffiti Alley is a good second stop for close-up street-art frames, and the Kensington Parking Garage gives a skyline panorama over the rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the car or a bright mural to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the colours stay rich and the sky doesn't wash out. In the narrow alley, try Live Photos to catch people walking through the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day, on a weekday, is usually calmer. Pedestrian Sundays from May to October bring large crowds that can block views along Augusta Avenue. The Garden Car is only out in warmer months.

text.access_note: The streets are open public space, but the Garden Car is seasonal and rooftop access at the Kensington Parking Garage is not confirmed, so check the official site or locally before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early on a weekday is usually quieter than later in the day or at weekends.
The ultra-wide lens helps in a narrow alley where you cannot step back.
A telephoto lens will bring the CN Tower closer in a skyline view from the garage.

name: Allan Gardens Conservatory
label: Allan Gardens
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jarvis Street and Carlton Street corner' (1 web pages); placed at crossing of Jarvis Street and Carlton Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/33405981: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Allan Gardens Conservatory' (150 m across).

text.description:
Allan Gardens Conservatory is a cluster of glass greenhouses in a city park, just east of Jarvis Street. The centrepiece is the Palm House, a glass-and-iron domed building completed in 1910 after a fire in 1902 destroyed the earlier pavilion on the site. Altogether the conservatory covers about 1,500 square metres and has six greenhouses, with wings added in the 1920s, in 1956-57 and in 2003. The park itself goes back to land given to the Toronto Horticultural Society in 1858, and it opened to the public in 1860. It was renamed Allan Gardens in 1901.

It photographs well because the pale glass roofs stand out against the trees and lawns, and the dome gives you a clear shape to build a picture around. The best approach shot comes as you enter from the Jarvis Street and Carlton Street corner, where the Palm House canopy and its wings first rise above the park. Frame it with a path or a few trees in the foreground so the building sits comfortably in its setting. Inside, the glass dome seen from below, ringed by palms and tropical plants, is the other picture to look for. Quick personal photos are fine, but longer shoots that need set-up have to be booked. Stay on the paths and keep out of the plant beds. Some exterior work may be under way, so check the City of Toronto page before you go.
text.geographic_location: Allan Gardens Conservatory sits in the Garden District of Toronto, inside Allan Gardens park. The park is bounded by Carlton Street to the north, Sherbourne Street to the east, Gerrard Street to the south and Jarvis Street to the west.
text.directions_text: From College station on the Line 1 subway, walk east for about 650 m (roughly 8 minutes on foot) to reach the conservatory. From the Church Street stop (streetcar 306, 501, 503, 505 and 506) the conservatory is about 540 m to the north-east, roughly 7 minutes on foot. From the Sherbourne Street stop (same streetcars) it is about 550 m to the north-west, also roughly 7 minutes on foot. For the approach shot, go first to the Jarvis Street and Carlton Street corner at the north-west of the park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the approach shot of the Palm House and its wings. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) inside the dome to fit in the palms and the curve of the glass. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the roof ribs or single plants.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Jarvis Street and Carlton Street (walk west from the corner into the park). The large glass-and-metal Palm House canopy and its extended wings rising above the park as you enter from the Jarvis side. From here the large glass-and-metal canopy and its wings rise above the park, which makes a good approach shot. text.description: Union Station is Toronto's grand railway hall, and from Front Street West it reads as one long, perfectly symmetrical wall of pale limestone. The central colonnade has 22 columns, each about 12 m high, and the whole building stretches roughly 229 m along the street. That gives you strong lines, repeating shapes and a natural frame. It was built in 1927 in the Beaux-Arts style and has been a National Historic Site of Canada since 1975. This is the classic view. The columns work like a frame around the entrance, and in the evening the lighting on the stonework makes the scene especially rewarding. Front Street is busy, so wait for gaps in the traffic and the pedestrians before you shoot. If you have a few minutes spare, walk to the corner of Bay Street and Front Street West. From there you look south-west along the building, and the CN Tower can sometimes be seen behind it, depending on the weather. Inside, the vaulted Great Hall ceiling is a good wide shot from the middle of the floor.
text.geographic_location: Union Station is in downtown Toronto on Front Street West, between Bay Street and York Street, with the Fairmont Royal York Hotel directly across the street. The Entertainment District begins just across Bay Street.
text.directions_text: Streetcar 509 also stops at Union Station, about 3 minutes on foot away. Once outside, stay on the street side facing the building so the whole facade is ahead of you to the south. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the kerb or the pavement so the whole colonnade fits. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close or want to include more sky, and keep the phone level so the columns don't lean. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the column tops and the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Front Street West (west of Bay Street, facing the main facade). The full recently restored main facade with its central colonnade, which can be framed dramatically, especially at night under architectural lighting. The photo shows the whole restored front with its central colonnade as a frame. This is the classic head-on view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the centre of the entrance up with the middle of the frame, so the symmetry does the work. Keep the phone upright and level to keep the vertical lines straight. Wait for a gap in the traffic and the pedestrians. For a different angle, walk to the corner of Bay Street and Front Street West and shoot south-west along the facade, with the CN Tower in the background if it is visible.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the lit stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lights don't burn out. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body, or rest the phone on a solid surface, to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, when the building is lit, gives the most dramatic result. Daytime also works well because the pale limestone shows its detail clearly.

text.access_note: The Front Street and Bay Street viewpoints are public pavements, but Union Station is a busy working transport hub, so check the official site before you go for anything inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Evening and night are good times because the facade is lit at night (stated in the viewpoint notes, not in the main sources).
A phone snapshot inside the station does not need a permit, according to the City of Toronto (viewpoint notes).

name: Nathan Phillips Square and the Toronto Sign

text.description: Nathan Phillips Square is the wide public forecourt of Toronto's New City Hall, and the lit TORONTO sign is its favourite photo stop. The letters stand about three metres tall and are raised above the water, with the curved City Hall towers rising behind them. The square opened in 1965 and was designed by the City Hall architect Viljo Revell with landscape architect Richard Strong. At 4.85 hectares, it is Canada's largest city square. The sign itself is usually busy, so this map suggests a calmer angle from the corner of Queen Street West and Bay Street, looking west. From there the illuminated towers and the sign sit in the distance, and the moving traffic in front adds streaks of light after dark. It makes a more dramatic picture than a straight shot from inside the crowd. If you want the close-up as well, the sign is just along the way, with the towers behind it. In winter the reflecting pool becomes a skating rink, which changes the foreground around the sign. The letters are sometimes changed for events, so the colours can vary from visit to visit. Guides disagree on exactly where the sign sits in the square, so check its spot on the map before you walk over.
text.geographic_location: In downtown Toronto, in front of New City Hall, where Queen Street West meets Bay Street. The square is the open plaza between the City Hall towers and the street.
text.directions_text: From Osgoode station (Line 1 subway), the sign is to the north-east, about 5 minutes on foot. From Queen station (Line 1 subway), it is to the west, also about 5 minutes on foot. Streetcar 501 stops at 160 York Street, about 5 minutes on foot to the south of the sign. Streetcars 306, 503, 505 and 506 stop at Bay Street, about 340 m (a few minutes on foot) to the north of the sign, so the sign is to the south of that stop. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the towers, the sign and the traffic in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) if you want to pull the sign and the towers closer without moving.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Queen Street West and Bay Street (facing west toward the City Hall towers). The illuminated City Hall towers and the sign in the distance, with light trails from street traffic in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the towers on one side third of the frame, with the road leading the eye toward them. Keep the phone level so the towers don't lean. For a close-up of the sign with the towers behind it, walk into the square afterwards. In winter, include the skating rink as foreground if it is there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, use night mode and hold the phone very still, braced against a railing or post, so passing traffic shows as soft light trails. Tap on the lit towers to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights don't wash out. During the day, use the default lens (1x) with gridlines.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk and the hour after it, when the towers are lit and the traffic is still busy, give the best mood. Daytime works well for a clear, bright shot of the sign.

text.access_note: Nathan Phillips Square is a public square owned by the City of Toronto, but events can change what is set up, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: A phone in night mode can record moving traffic as light trails if it is held steady.
Bracing the phone against a railing or lamp post at the corner helps keep night shots sharp.

The sign area is usually busy with visitors.

name: Toronto Islands and the skyline view
label: Toronto Islands
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Centre Island Pier' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Centre Island Pier' (way/985659382): middle (134 m across); moved 35 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/10705563: large area 'Toronto Islands' (5126 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description: The Toronto Islands are a chain of 15 small islands in Lake Ontario, just off the downtown shore. They shelter Toronto Harbour, and they give you the best distance for a skyline photo: the whole city lined up across open water. The islands were once a sandy peninsula and became true islands after a violent storm in 1858. Today they hold parkland, beaches and a car-free residential community, the largest of its kind in an urban area in North America. From there you face north across the harbour and see a wide sweep of downtown, with the CN Tower and the Financial District towers. It is a more sweeping view than the usual island postcard. Because the towers sit a good way off, the water in front does a lot of the work. Keep some of it in the frame and the skyline looks calm and orderly, not crowded. Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full sweep, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier picture. If you have time, Olympic Island Park gives another open view of the CN Tower and Rogers Centre. Hanlan's Point offers a less usual angle that includes passing planes.
text.geographic_location: The Toronto Islands lie in Lake Ontario just south of downtown Toronto, across the harbour from the waterfront. Centre Island has a pier whose end looks north across the harbour at the city.
text.directions_text: From downtown Toronto, make your way to Jack Layton Ferry Terminal on the harbour front. Take the public ferry to the islands and check the ferry schedule on the official ferry site before you go. From the ferry landing, follow the paths to Centre Island Pier and walk to its far end. Do not use the pedestrian tunnel to the airport, as it leads to a secure area and not to the parks. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole skyline from the end of the pier. Then use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the CN Tower and the nearby towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Centre Island Pier (end of the pier, facing north across the harbour). A wide sweep of the downtown skyline across the harbour, with the CN Tower and Financial District towers in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the horizon up with one of them so the water and city stay level. Leave a band of water in the bottom third of the frame to give the towers some space. For a different version, try Olympic Island Park for a clear view of the CN Tower and Rogers Centre, or Hanlan's Point for an angle that includes planes.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the towers to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Panorama mode can also work well on the pier, so move slowly and keep the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, roughly 4 to 7 p.m., when the western sun lights the glass of the city's towers.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is a free, open-air public space, but you need the public ferry from Jack Layton Ferry Terminal (a fare applies), so check the official ferry site for schedules before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: From the end of Centre Island Pier the skyline is far enough away that the towers look small, so the ultra-wide or a telephoto zoom helps.
A band of water in the foreground helps the composition, and gridlines help keep the horizon level.
Light from the west in late afternoon falls on the front of the city's buildings when viewed from the pier.

text.description:
Toronto Music Garden is a public park on Toronto's waterfront, along Queens Quay West. What makes it work for a phone is the mix of soft planting, curved paths and a city skyline just behind. From the kerb on Queens Quay West you can catch a streetcar passing in front of the garden. Keep the tram slightly blurred and the greenery sharp, and the picture says as much about the city as about the park.

Inside the garden there are two more pictures worth taking. From the amphitheatre steps, the CN Tower rises above the curved paths and grasses. The round wrought-iron Music Pavilion also makes a good foreground, with the downtown towers standing behind it. If you only have time for one, start then walk in for the others.

The garden is free to enter. Take casual phone photos as you would in any park. If you are planning a group or commercial shoot, permit rules may apply, so check with the City first.

On the street side, stay on the pavement and watch for traffic and trams while you wait for the right moment. Inside, step aside to let others pass while you line up a shot. Overcast days suit the greenery well, because the colours stay even and the sky is easy to expose.
text.geographic_location: The garden is on Queens Quay West, along Toronto's waterfront, just east of the Spadina Avenue streetcar stop.
text.directions_text: The nearest Line 1 subway stop is St. Andrew station, about 18 minutes on foot to the south-west; Union station is a similar distance. For a shorter walk, streetcar 509 stops at Spadina Avenue; Queens Quay West (about 4 minutes on foot, to the west) and at Dan Leckie Way (about 3 minutes on foot, to the east). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the streetcar in front of the garden. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) inside for the pavilion with the towers behind. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the CN Tower closer from the amphitheatre steps.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Queens Quay West (curb along the garden's edge). A streetcar passing in motion blur in front of the garden, a city-life counterpoint to the green space. For a second view, go into the garden: from the amphitheatre steps the CN Tower rises above the curved paths and grasses, and the round Music Pavilion in the foreground has the downtown towers behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the garden's greenery on the lower third, with the streetcar crossing the middle. Keep your elbows tucked in and wait for a tram to arrive. For the CN Tower, place it on a vertical grid line and let the curving path lead the eye towards it. Take a few frames of each so you can pick the best.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the garden to focus and drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. For the streetcar, take a Live Photo or a quick burst and choose the frame with the nicest blur. Keep the phone steady against your body or a solid support.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the planting and the towers than harsh midday sun. An overcast day also works well for the garden itself.

text.access_note: The garden is a public park that is free to enter, but permit rules for group or commercial shoots can vary, so check the official site before you go.

text.description: High Park is one of Toronto's largest parks, and it makes a good change of pace from the city streets. It opened to the public in 1876 on land left to the city by John George Howard, and it covers 161 hectares. About a third of it is still natural, including a rare oak savannah. For photos, the best place to start is Grenadier Pond on the western edge. The pond covers 14.2 hectares, so there is plenty of open water. On a calm day it reflects the trees along the shore, and you get blossom in spring and autumn colour in the fall. The path at pond level is also a quieter option than the busier hilltop areas. Two other spots are worth a look if you have time. The Maple Leaf Flower Bed has a red maple-leaf-shaped planting in the foreground, with hedges, trees and the lake behind. Hillside Gardens has rows of pink cherry trees, which are only worth visiting from late April to early May. On the hillside along the pond's eastern shore you will find the gardens and a grove of cherry trees. Keep to the paths, and do not pull branches or climb trees for a picture. Leave the shot to the view, and let the water do the work: a low, steady phone held near the edge of the path gives the cleanest reflections.
text.geographic_location: High Park lies west of downtown Toronto, stretching south from Bloor Street West to The Queensway, just north of Lake Ontario. Grenadier Pond forms its western edge, near Ellis Park Road.
text.directions_text: One easy way is streetcar 506 to High Park Loop, the nearest tram stop, then about 8 minutes on foot heading south-west into the park. You can also take the Line 2 subway to High Park station, about 15 minutes on foot to the middle of the park, or to Keele station, about 18 minutes on foot. From the middle of the park, Grenadier Pond is on the western side, near Ellis Park Road and Valleymede Road. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole pond and the trees along the shore. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, more natural look at the reflections. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a patch of blossom or autumn colour on the far bank.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Grenadier Pond (lakeshore near Ellis Park Road and Valleymede Road). The pond's water and reflections of the surrounding trees, with blossoms or autumn colour across the shore. From here you look across the pond's water, with the trees reflected in it and the blossom or autumn colour along the shore. The middle of High Park lies to the north-east of this spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the water's edge on the lower third line, so the reflections fill the frame. Include a little shoreline or a branch in the foreground for depth. For a second view, try the Maple Leaf Flower Bed, with the red leaf shape in the foreground and the lake behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or the trees to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out and the colours stay rich. Hold the phone steady, or lean on a railing or post, so the reflections stay sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, or about 1.5 hours before sunset. For blossom, go in late April to early May. Autumn colour also works well here.

text.access_note: High Park is an open public park, but commercial photography needs a permit and weekend car access is restricted, so check the City of Toronto site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Reflections on the pond are usually clearest when the water is calm and there is little wind.
A low, steady phone and gridlines help keep reflections level; leaning on a railing or post can reduce shake.
Turning the exposure slider down slightly can protect the sky from over-exposure in bright conditions.

name: Trinity Bellwoods Park
label: Trinity Bellwoods
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Trinity Bellwoods Gates' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/16751345: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Trinity Bellwoods Park' (763 m across).

text.description:
Trinity Bellwoods Park is a big, much-loved public park in west-central Toronto, covering 15.4 hectares between Queen Street West and Dundas Street. For photos, the best place to start is the stone gateway at the Queen Street West entrance. It is the only part of the old Trinity College that survives. The college opened here in 1852, moved away after federation with the University of Toronto, and most of its buildings were pulled down in the early 1950s. The ironwork you see today is a replica, and the original is now in Port Hope, Ontario. That history gives you a solid frame for a simple shot: the gateway in the foreground, with the path and trees leading away behind it.

Beyond the gates, the park sits in a shallow bowl that was once the Garrison Creek ravine, so the lawns dip gently and the mature trees make good layers in a photo. Locals come here to walk dogs, picnic and play sports. The park is also known for its white squirrels, which can make a fun close-up if you are patient. Walk a little way in and turn round for a different view back toward the gateway.

For practical photo advice, arrive when the entrance is quiet if you can, and stand square to the gates so the posts look straight. People walking through add scale and life. The gates have been fenced off for repairs in the past, so it is worth checking they are open before you make a special trip.
text.geographic_location: Trinity Bellwoods Park is in west-central Toronto, between Queen Street West to the south and Dundas Street to the north. The gates are at the Queen Street West entrance on the park's south side.
text.directions_text: The easiest way is to take streetcar 501 to the Shaw Street stop, which is close to the park, about 200 m from the middle of it. Streetcar 505 also stops there. Claremont Street (streetcar 501) is another option, on the west side of the park. From Christie station (Line 2 subway) it is about 1.8 km on foot, so the streetcar is simpler. Head for the Queen Street West entrance on the south side of the park, where the gates stand. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to frame the gateway with the path and trees behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the gateway and the surrounding trees, but keep the gates near the centre so the edges do not stretch them. Try 2x or more for a tighter shot of the gateway details or the tree-lined path.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the gateway shot, walk south from there to the Queen Street West entrance at the Trinity Bellwoods Gates, stand just inside the gates and face north. The photo shows the stone and iron gateway framing the park's southern path and trees, with the park interior behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on your gridlines and line the gate posts up with the vertical lines so they stand straight. Keep the path in the middle to lead the eye into the park. If you want a variation, a view of the CN Tower from the park's south-east corner is another option, though that corner has no name.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky behind the trees is washing out. Try a Live Photo so you can pick the best frame as people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to early evening in summer is a pleasant time, with softer light and a lively park. Early morning is usually quieter if you want the gateway without people.

text.access_note: The park is open public space, but check the official City of Toronto site before you go in case of repair work or fencing near the gates.
claims_not_in_sources: Late afternoon to early evening light in summer is softer and more flattering (a single travel guide suggests roughly 6-8 p.m. on summer weekdays; this is not specific to the gates).
Early morning is usually quieter at the park entrance.
Facing north from the Queen Street West entrance, the sun is mostly behind or beside you through the day, so the gateway tends to be front-lit.
A view of the CN Tower can be had from the park's south-east corner.

name: Old City Hall
label: Old City Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Nathan Phillips Square' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Nathan Phillips Square' (way/198500757): middle (359 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3116: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Old City Hall' (153 m across).

text.description: Old City Hall is a big Romanesque civic building of sandstone and other stone in three colours, finished in 1899. It was the home of Toronto's city council until 1966 and then served as a court house until 2023. Its clock tower, which stands 103.6 metres high after the restoration, is the part everyone photographs. The tower sits off-centre on the front, and it closes the view along Bay Street from Front Street. The building photographs well because the texture is so rich: arches, carved stone, bronze gargoyles (replicas added in 2002) and, if you look under the eaves, the architect's name carved into the stonework all the way round. It was designated a National Historic Site in 1984. It was nearly demolished in the 1960s for a shopping scheme, but public protest saved it, and the Eaton Centre was built around it instead. The modern City Hall and its pool sit just across the street, so you can set old and new in one frame. At the foot of the steps on Queen Street is the Cenotaph, put up in 1925. The best view is from the square opposite, where you can fit the whole width of the facade in. Walk closer afterwards for details of the stonework and the tower.
text.geographic_location: In Downtown Toronto, on the corner of Queen and Bay streets, directly across Bay Street from Nathan Phillips Square and the present City Hall. The Eaton Centre was built right beside it.
text.directions_text: The nearest Line 1 subway stop is Queen station, and the building is about 3 minutes on foot to the west of it. From Osgoode station on Line 1 subway it is about 6-7 minutes on foot, heading north-east. If you arrive by streetcar, get off at Bay Street (streetcar 306, 503, 505 or 506) and walk about 5 minutes with the building to the south of the stop. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full width of the facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the pool and square in the foreground. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the clock tower, gargoyles and carved stone.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Nathan Phillips Square (across Queen Street from the building, near the reflecting pool and the TORONTO sign). The full width of the Romanesque facade with the clock tower rising above the centre, with the modern City Hall towers and the pool in the foreground. Old City Hall lies to the east from here. This is the classic postcard angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it does not lean. Hold the phone level, as tilting upwards bends the building. Use the pool or the TORONTO sign as a foreground to give a sense of scale. Then walk across the street for close-ups of the carved stone and gargoyles with the telephoto lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out and the tower keeps its colour. If the pool is still, try a shot that includes its reflection.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Try a bright, clear day when the sun is on the front of the building, or a softer hour near sunset for warmer stone. Early morning is usually quieter on the square.

text.access_note: The outside of the building can be photographed from the public pavements and from Nathan Phillips Square; for going inside, check the official site before you go, as the courts have moved out.
claims_not_in_sources: The front of the building faces Queen Street (south), so it tends to get direct sun through much of the day.
Early morning is usually quieter on Nathan Phillips Square.
A still reflecting pool can give a reflection of the buildings.
Tilting a phone upwards makes tall buildings appear to lean inwards.

name: Graffiti Alley
label: Graffiti Alley
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rush Lane' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Rush Lane and Portland Street (our map tiles).

text.description: Graffiti Alley is a long lane lined with murals and wall art, and it works well for phone photos because the paintings fill both sides and pull the eye down the lane. From the Rush Lane corner you get a long run of murals receding ahead of you, which gives pictures a strong sense of depth. Walk on and you can also take a close, straight-on shot of the full aquarium mural, which wraps across the window sashes of a building. The walls are described as unofficial rather than designated legal graffiti walls, so what you see can change, and parked vehicles sometimes hide parts of the art. Construction can also block the road at times. Expect weekend crowds and buskers. If people keep walking into your frame, step back a little and shoot from farther away rather than waiting for a clear gap. A good plan is to start at Rush Lane and walk east, so you meet the art in a sensible order. Go early in the morning if you can, when fewer people are about. Another good spot is the entrance from Augusta Avenue, where the first murals open up along the lane ahead. Neither the aquarium building nor the Augusta entrance has an official name, so use the street names and look for the artwork when you navigate.
text.geographic_location: Graffiti Alley is a lane of murals in central Toronto, a short walk from the Spadina Avenue streetcar stop. It is reached from Rush Lane and from Augusta Avenue.
text.directions_text: The easiest start is the Spadina Avenue streetcar stop (streetcar 501, among others), about 350 m away, with the alley to the south. The Peter Street stop (streetcar 501) is also about 350 m away, with the alley to the west. From Osgoode station on the Line 1 subway it is about 1 km on foot, heading west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the long view down the lane, then switch to the default lens (1x) for the aquarium mural. Try the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out a single mural and keep passers-by out of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Rush Lane and Portland Street (corner at the east end of the alley, then walk east back along the murals). A long run of murals receding down the lane, with the alley's wall art filling the frame. From here the murals run away from you down the lane and the wall art fills the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the lane up with the lines so the walls look straight. Keep the lane's perspective leading into the distance, and wait for a quiet moment rather than cropping people out afterwards. For the aquarium mural, stand square on and keep the phone level so the window sashes stay straight. The Augusta Avenue entrance is a good alternative if you want the first murals opening up ahead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright part of a mural to set focus, then use the exposure slider to stop the sky or light walls washing out. Ultra-wide shots can bend straight edges near the corners, so keep important details away from the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when foot traffic is lighter.

name: Gooderham Building (Flatiron)
label: Gooderham Building

text.description:
The Gooderham Building, also called the Flatiron Building, is a red-brick office building completed in 1892 at 49 Wellington Street East. It is wedged into the point where Front Street and Wellington Street meet, so it has a very narrow, rounded wedge shape. It was designed by David Roberts Jr. for the distiller George Gooderham Sr., and the Gooderham and Worts distillery used it as offices until 1952. It still works as an office building today.

It photographs well because the shape is so clear against the taller buildings around it. Look for the steep copper roof with its dormers and the arched windows on the upper floors. The back wall carries a large trompe-l'œil mural by Derek Michael Besant, which shows the Perkins Building across the street and makes the wall look as though it has extra windows. The view along Front Street towards the rounded corner, with the heritage blocks on either side and the Financial District towers behind, often appears in pictures of the city. The CN Tower can also be seen from some angles.

Berczy Park, with its dog fountain, is just behind the building, so it is worth looking at the park too. Allow a few minutes to walk around and compare angles before you settle on one.
text.geographic_location: In downtown Toronto, on the eastern edge of the Financial District, in the St. Lawrence neighbourhood. It sits on the triangular block where Front Street and Wellington Street East meet, just east of Yonge Street.
text.directions_text: King station (Line 1 subway) is about 286 m away, to the west of the building, so walk east from the station. Union station (Line 1 subway) is about 565 m away, with the building to the north-east of the station. Streetcar 503 stops at Wellington Street East, about 48 m from the building, and at Yonge Street, King Station, about 4 minutes on foot away. The phone icon on the map is about 50 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from where you stand, which takes in the whole building comfortably. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you step closer or want the street and the sky included. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the copper roof, the dormers and the mural.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 50 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. From here the whole wedge shape is in view. Then walk a little along Front Street to try the view down the street towards the rounded corner.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the building's edge up with a vertical line so the walls stay straight. Keep your phone level, because tilting it makes the tall walls lean. For the street view, let the older buildings frame both sides and the towers rise behind. The mural and cornice make good close-up photos with the telephoto lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the brick to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out and the red stays rich. Take a few shots, as people and streetcars will pass through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light, or a bright overcast day, shows the brick colour well and avoids harsh shadows. Early mornings and weekends are likely to be quieter in this office area.

text.access_note: You can see and photograph the outside from public streets and the nearby park, but it is a working office building, so check the official site before you go if you hope to go inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon light or overcast skies suit red brick and reduce harsh shadows.
The area is likely to be quieter on early mornings and weekends because it is an office district.

text.description: Riverdale Park East is a public park, and this spot is its skyline view: you look west and take in Toronto's city centre as a distant band of towers. A skyline shot like this works best when you treat the buildings as the backdrop. Put whatever foreground is available in the frame, and the towers read as a long way off but still clear. Stand at the phone icon on the map, then face west. From there the view runs towards the downtown towers. Take a few frames at different heights. Standing upright gives you more of the skyline, while crouching a little lowers the horizon and gives the foreground more room in the frame. Check the edges of the frame for lamp posts, bins and branches, because they can cut across a distant skyline. If people walk through your shot, wait a moment or shift a step to one side. If the sky looks flat, put more of the foreground in the frame. If the sky has cloud or colour, give it more room.
text.geographic_location: Riverdale Park East is in Toronto's Riverdale area, east of the city centre. The skyline view looks west.
text.directions_text: From Broadview station (Line 2 subway, also served by streetcar 505), the park is about 800 m away. Alternatively, take streetcar 505 to the Withrow Avenue stop, which is about 170 m west of the view's subject. The phone icon on the map is about 120 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the skyline. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more foreground and sky, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the towers closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 120 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. The skyline is in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the lower or upper third line. Keep the towers in the middle third and use whatever lines the foreground offers as a leading line. Hold the phone level so the towers stay upright. A zoomed shot at 2x or 3x gives a compressed view of the skyline, while the default lens (1x) shows more of the surroundings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the towers to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky looks washed out. Try a panorama if you want the full width of the view, and move the phone slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening usually gives softer light on the skyline, and after sunset you can try night mode. Rest your elbows against your body or lean on something firm to keep the phone steady.

text.access_note: This is a public park, but check the City of Toronto's official site before you go for any closures or events.

The skyline view looks towards downtown Toronto.

label: Fort York
camera_source: Commons cluster (52 photos).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/13740577: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fort York' (441 m across).

text.description:
Fort York is an early 19th-century military fort that once guarded the entrance to Toronto Harbour. Its stone-lined earthwork walls enclose eight historical buildings, two of them blockhouses. That mix of low grassy ramparts, plain timber and stone buildings and open sky suits a phone camera well, because you can fit a lot into one frame without fuss.

The story helps you choose your shots. A British garrison was established here in 1793. American forces destroyed the original fort after the Battle of York in April 1813, and it was rebuilt between 1813 and 1815. It was designated a National Historic Site of Canada in 1923 and restored to its early-19th-century look in 1934. The fort sits within a 16.6 hectare (41-acre) historic site that also takes in Garrison Common, military cemeteries and a visitor centre, so there is plenty of room to wander and look for new angles.

Start with a wide shot of the walls and buildings together, then move closer for details such as a blockhouse, a doorway or the line of an earthwork bank. Keep the horizon level using the gridlines, and take a few frames of the same view so you can pick the best one later. Walking a short loop inside the walls will give you more variety than staying in one place.
text.geographic_location: Fort York is in the Fort York neighbourhood of Toronto and once defended the entrance to Toronto Harbour. The surrounding historic site includes Garrison Common and a visitor centre.
text.directions_text: Bastion Street stop on the same streetcar lines is a little further away. From St. Andrew station (Line 1 subway) it is about 1.8 km on foot (roughly 20 to 25 minutes), heading south-west. The phone icon on the map is about 190 m north-east of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full sweep of the walls and buildings, and the default lens (1x) for most general views. Try 2x or more, if your phone has it, for blockhouse details and rooflines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 190 m north-east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Turn to face south-west and take your first frame, then walk in to look for the walls and the two blockhouses.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use the line of a wall or earthwork bank to lead the eye towards a building. Crouch slightly with the ultra-wide to make the grass and ramparts feel bigger. For people-free shots, wait a moment for visitors to move out of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building you care about to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky looks washed out. Take a quick panorama along a stretch of wall, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the walls. Check the official site for visiting times before you go.

text.access_note: Fort York is a National Historic Site with a visitor centre, so access to parts of it may be ticketed or restricted: check the official site before you go.

text.description: Sugar Beach is a small sandy beach-style park on Toronto's central waterfront, and it is a cheerful place to take photos. The scene is built from bold, simple shapes: pale sand, open water and the harbour beyond. That mix of sand and water gives your pictures a clear sense of place that a plain skyline shot lacks. From there you can fit the sand and the water into one frame, with people adding scale. Walk down onto the sand afterwards for lower, closer shots. Keep the horizon level using your phone's gridlines, and check that the edges of the frame are clear of stray bags or bins. On a busy day, wait a moment for a gap in the crowd, or let a few people stay in the shot to give it life. Try going when it is quieter if you want a clearer view.
text.geographic_location: Sugar Beach is on Toronto's central waterfront, on the harbour side of the city's downtown, roughly 800 m east of the Queens Quay Island Ferry Docks stop.
text.directions_text: The nearest tram stop is Wellington Street East (streetcar 503), about 790 m on foot, with the beach to the south-east. Queens Quay - Island Ferry Docks (streetcar 509) is about 790 m away, with the beach to the east. Union station on the Line 1 subway is about 1.05 km away, to the east, and King station on the Line 1 subway is about 1.03 km away, to the south-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full beach scene. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close to the sand and want it to fill the frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details or people on the sand without walking into them.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (on the sand, facing the umbrellas with the Redpath factory behind). The pink umbrellas and Muskoka chairs on the white sand, with the Redpath Sugar factory silhouette and the lake or skyline behind. This gives a wide view of the whole scene. For close-ups, walk towards the sand afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on a lower or upper line, not the middle. Use the edge of the sand or the waterline as a lead-in. Crouch a little for the ultra-wide close shots so the sand fills the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the sand to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white sand does not wash out. Try Live Photos to catch a person walking through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Mornings and the hour before sunset usually give softer light and fewer people. Midday sun on pale sand can be harsh, so use the exposure slider.

text.access_note: Sugar Beach is a public waterfront space, but check the official City of Toronto site before you go for any closures or event restrictions.
